data.title: Callback Phishing (Telephone-Oriented Attack Delivery)
data.summary: Messages containing no link or attachment, only a telephone number and a plausible pretext, led staff to call attacker-operated support lines and follow instructions — including installing remote access software.
data.description:
Callback phishing defeats mail security by containing nothing to detect: a plain message about a subscription renewal or an unexpected invoice, with a number to call to dispute it.

The victim initiates the call, which inverts the usual suspicion — they chose to make contact, so the person answering is treated as legitimate. A practised operator then walks them through installing a remote access tool, which is a legitimate signed product and therefore unlikely to be blocked.

The result is interactive access to a corporate workstation with the user's cooperation, and often their assistance in bypassing a prompt the security tooling raises.
data.recommendation:
* Publish how IT and finance contact staff, and state that support will never ask for remote access following an inbound message.
* Restrict installation of remote access tooling, and alert on it appearing on a workstation.
* Give staff a single internal number to verify any unexpected request, and make that reflex the training.
* Include no-link pretexts in simulations; a programme that only measures clicks does not measure this at all.
data.short_recommendation: Publish how support contacts staff, and verify callbacks independently.
